title: IBM Z and LinuxONE Dual-ISA Processor and AI Acceleration at Hot Chips 2026
gist: IBM disclosed a 2nm mainframe processor with 11 cores at 5.7+ GHz whose single core natively executes both z/Architecture and AArch64 in hardware, plus a second-generation AI inference accelerator with 16 active cores, 96GB HBM3e at ~4TB/s and FP4 support. The bet is to import the entire Arm software ecosystem onto Z rather than defend a closed platform.

themes.theme: Dual-ISA silicon as an ecosystem land grab

insights.claim: IBM's next mainframe processor carries 11 IBM Z cores at 5.7+ GHz on a 2nm process where each core can natively execute both z/Architecture and AArch64.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: IBM is committing leading-edge 2nm capacity to mainframe silicon, a signal that Z remains a high-margin franchise worth defending with the best process available.
insights.quote: This chip carries 11 IBM Z cores at 5.7+ GHz on a 2nm process, and each core can natively execute both z/Architecture and AArch64.
insights.locator: Now comes the core of the announcement

insights.claim: IBM implemented AArch64 in full hardware rather than through translation, with a little-endian Arm implementation alongside big-endian z/Architecture, AArch64 v9.3, SVE and SVE2 support, and 2,792 implemented AArch64 instructions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Full hardware implementation removes the performance penalty that killed prior binary-translation bridges, making Arm workload migration onto Z credible rather than aspirational.
insights.quote: A key choice here is that IBM implemented AArch64 in full hardware rather than through translation.
insights.locator: A key choice here is that IBM implemented AArch64

insights.claim: IBM claims Arm SystemReady compliance so that Arm software sees a native Arm processor and runs unmodified, out-of-the-box, on a standard Arm platform.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Determines whether IBM can absorb the off-the-shelf Arm software base without ISV porting spend, which is the whole economic case for the design.
insights.quote: Arm software sees a native Arm processor. Arm runs unmodified, out-of-the-box, and onto a standard Arm platform.
insights.locator: IBM also claims Arm SystemReady compliance

insights.claim: The 2,792 implemented AArch64 instructions are more than twice the number of Z instructions, undercutting the notion that RISC ISAs are inherently smaller than CISC ones.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A reminder that Arm's ISA surface area is now enormous, raising the engineering bar for anyone claiming a clean-sheet Arm-compatible core.
insights.quote: IBM said the 2792 AArch64 instructions are more than twice the Z instructions.
insights.locator: IBM also claims Arm SystemReady compliance

insights.claim: IBM built one core that runs both ISAs rather than placing separate Z and Arm cores on the same die, and a thread can switch between s390x and Arm software in nanoseconds.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Nanosecond ISA switching enables mixed workloads inside one logical partition, a capability no other server vendor can currently offer.
insights.quote: this is not Z+Arm cores, this is Z and Arm in one core
insights.locator: Branch prediction shows how much of the existing Z core design

insights.claim: IBM reused much of the existing Z core for AArch64, consuming Arm's XML architecture descriptions via automation to feed decode, repurposing register rename for the GR16-31 range, and reusing CISC constructs such as memory copy and clear.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows the incremental engineering cost of dual-ISA was manageable, which means competitors could plausibly copy the approach.
insights.locator: Branch prediction shows how much of the existing Z core design

themes.theme: Cache, accelerators, and the Z system design

insights.claim: The processor pairs cores with 36MB private L2 caches joined into a virtual L3/L4, disclosed live as a 432MB Virtual-L3 and 3.5GB virtual L4, on an SMT=2 design.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Cache-heavy design is IBM's substitute for HBM on transaction workloads, a different silicon-cost profile from AI accelerators.
insights.quote: This is also a SMT=2 design and has a 432MB Virtual-L3 and 3.5GB virtual L4 cache. That was not on the slide we got, but they showed those specs live.
insights.locator: Now comes the core of the announcement

insights.claim: IBM exposes Z accelerators for crypto, GZIP compression, and the on-chip AI unit as platform devices to Linux on Arm with comparable latency to native Z instructions, while the Z ISA still exposes them as instructions for s390x workloads.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Arm workloads inherit mainframe accelerators without rewrites, a differentiator against commodity Arm servers.
insights.locator: On the software side, IBM exposes the Z accelerators

insights.claim: The design targets 99.999999% availability through error checking across arrays, dataflows and control, transparent recovery from transient faults, core sparing for persistent faults, concurrent repair, and RAIM memory protection.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The eight-nines availability target is the moat: it is what general-purpose cloud servers cannot match and what justifies mainframe pricing.
insights.locator: Reliability carries over to this design

insights.claim: IBM positions the two ISAs to coexist through Linux KVM and OpenShift Virtualization, with s390x Linux, ARM64 Linux, and z/OS logical partitions sharing the same processor.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Consolidation pitch: customers can retire separate Arm server fleets onto existing Z footprints.
insights.locator: Rather than forcing a single ecosystem

insights.claim: Something like 70% of the world's transaction volume goes over IBM Z mainframes, and IBM argues bringing in the Arm ecosystem brings a new class of applications onto that installed base.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the captive base IBM can upsell Arm-native software into, the revenue mechanism behind the dual-ISA bet.
insights.quote: Something like 70% of the world’s transaction volume goes over IBM Z mainframes.
insights.locator: IBM opened with the historical context for Z

insights.claim: IBM's second-generation AI inference accelerator packs 16 active AI cores plus one redundant core, with FP4 and MXFP4 datatypes IBM says can deliver up to 4x TOPS.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A redundant AI core is unique in the accelerator market and signals IBM selling AI reliability rather than peak throughput.
insights.quote: This chip packs 16 active AI cores plus one redundant core, with FP4 and MXFP4 datatypes that IBM says can deliver up to 4x TOPS. Amazing, this is AI with redundancy.

insights.claim: The accelerator adds 96GB of HBM3e running up to about 4TB/s, roughly 20x the memory bandwidth of the current generation, and uses PCIe Gen6 as a low-latency peer-to-peer interface.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: IBM is now an HBM buyer at scale, adding another enterprise bidder to already-tight HBM supply.
insights.quote: It adds 96GB of HBM3e running up to about 4TB/s, roughly 20x the memory bandwidth of the current generation

insights.claim: IBM positions the AI part for mission-critical work with confidential computing protecting data and models at rest, in transit, and in use, including quantum-safe cryptography and secure boot.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Targets regulated enterprise inference where model and data confidentiality, not tokens per second, drives purchasing.
insights.locator: On the security and resilience side

themes.theme: Strategic read on the mainframe's future

insights.claim: IBM's dual-ISA bet is a bid to keep the mainframe relevant as Arm software and AI workloads reshape the data center, rather than treating Z as a closed platform.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reframes IBM Z from a declining legacy franchise to a platform actively expanding its addressable workload set.
insights.quote: IBM’s dual-ISA bet is a bid to keep the mainframe relevant as Arm software and AI workloads reshape the data center, rather than treating Z as a closed platform.

insights.claim: How much of the surrounding Arm software stack runs unmodified on the dual-ISA core is the key open question for the design's commercial success.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The metric to watch before assigning value to the dual-ISA strategy is real-world unmodified Arm software coverage, not IBM's compliance claims.
insights.quote: How much of the surrounding Arm software stack runs unmodified on the core will be worth watching.

insights.claim: NVIDIA has been adopting similar mainframe-style reliability engineering, such as replacing many cables with PCB to increase system reliability.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reliability engineering is converging across mainframe and AI rack vendors, so RAS becomes a competitive axis in AI infrastructure too.
insights.quote: NVIDIA has been doing some similar things like replacing many cables with PCB to increase reliability of its systems.
insights.locator: Reliability carries over to this design
